llm_response.content:
Empirical Research Plan:  “The Causal Impact of Centralized School Assignment on Student Outcomes”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (FRD) implemented at the assignment cut-off(s).

Why FRD is appropriate  
• The centralized algorithm produces a sharp jump in the probability of receiving a seat at a more-preferred school at a known priority/lottery cut-off, but assignment is not perfectly deterministic because of tie-breakers and multi-school rankings ⇒ fuzzy, not sharp, RD.  
• Students cannot perfectly manipulate their random lottery number; therefore, observations just above and below the cut-off are locally comparable.  
• The FRD estimates a Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) for “marginal admittees” – exactly the policy-relevant group for seat reallocation.

Alternative designs (pure lottery IV across all ranks, DID with cohorts) are possible but deliver weaker or less transparent identifying assumptions than the RD that is built into the mechanism itself. We therefore treat the FRD as the primary design and use the lottery IV as a robustness/over-identification check.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition
-------------------------------------------------
• Running variable Rᵢ:  student i’s distance from the cut-off at her first-choice school in the assignment algorithm.  
 Rᵢ = (lottery draw or composite priority score) – (school-specific marginal admitted value).  
• Cut-off: Rᵢ = 0.  
• Treatment indicator Dᵢ:  1 if student is assigned to a school that is weakly higher on her preference list than the school she would have received absent crossing the cut-off (operationalized as “assigned to first-choice school” or, in robustness, “assigned within top k choices”).  
• Instrument Zᵢ:  1{Rᵢ ≤ 0}.  Crossing the threshold raises Pr(Dᵢ = 1) but does not force Dᵢ = 1 ⇒ fuzzy RD.  
• Control group:  students with 0 < Rᵢ ≤ h (just below the cut-off) who are not admitted to the higher-ranked school.  
• Treatment timing:  the assignment letter is received in spring; outcomes (state test scores, GPA, graduation) are observed after at least one year of attendance, up to several years for attainment outcomes.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes in R at the cut-off.  
 Plausibility: R is generated from a centralized random lottery plus deterministic priorities (siblings, distance). Within narrow bandwidths, families cannot fine-tune R; thus potential outcomes should be smooth.

A2. No precise manipulation of R around the cut-off (no sorting).  
 Plausibility: lottery numbers are truly random; priorities (e.g., sibling) are predetermined. We can validate with McCrary density test and balance checks.

A3. Exclusion restriction (FRD version): crossing the cut-off affects outcomes only through its impact on being admitted to the more-preferred school.  
 Plausibility: the only mechanical effect of R on schooling comes via seat offer. Still, need to rule out simultaneous changes in peer composition within the same school tier; use narrow bandwidth and covariate continuity tests.

A4. Monotonicity (first-stage sign is weakly positive for all students).  
 Plausibility: no student is less likely to get the seat by having a “better” lottery number.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): a student’s assignment status does not directly change classmates’ outcomes across the cut-off within the bandwidth.  
 Plausibility: bandwidth is tiny relative to school size; any peer externality is second-order.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
-------------------------------------------------
T1. Sorting / manipulation of running variable.  
 Check: McCrary density test; continuity of predetermined covariates; replicate using only pure lottery priorities where manipulation is impossible.

T2. Heterogeneous cut-offs across schools leading to varying “local” effects.  
 Solution: estimate school-by-school FRDs and aggregate via inverse-variance weights; or implement pooled FRD with school fixed effects and cluster-robust SEs.

T3. Attrition or outcome measurement error (e.g., students move districts).  
 Solution: use intent-to-treat (ITT) in sharp RD as robustness; bound estimates with Lee-bounds; create balanced panel where pre-treatment test score exists; include indicator for missing outcomes as dependent variable placebo.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(rdrobust)    # RD estimation
library(fixest)      # IV & high-dim FE
library(sandwich)    # vcov functions
library(modelsummary)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and clean data
# -------------------------------------------------
dat <- read_csv("school_assignment_data.csv") %>% 
  mutate(
    # Running variable: margin relative to cut-off for first-choice school
    margin = lottery_score - school_cutoff_score,    
    # Instrument: 1 if margin ≤ 0  (got offer)
    z_offer = if_else(margin <= 0, 1, 0),
    # Treatment: actually attends more-preferred school (top choice)
    treat = assigned_top_choice,                   
    # Center running variable at zero for plotting
    margin_c = margin                                 
  )

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Main fuzzy RD (local polynomial, rdrobust)
# -------------------------------------------------
rd_main <- rdrobust(
  y = dat$test_score_post,   # outcome (e.g., math score 1 yr later)
  x = dat$margin_c,
  fuzzy = dat$z_offer,
  p = 1,           # linear
  h = NULL         # MSE-optimal bandwidth
)

summary(rd_main)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Equivalent 2SLS using local bandwidth for transparency
# -------------------------------------------------
bw <- rd_main$bws[1, 1]  # left/right same order
dat_local <- dat %>% filter(abs(margin_c) <= bw)

iv_fit <- feols(
  test_score_post ~ treat | z_offer,   # 2SLS syntax
  data = dat_local,
  cluster = ~school_id                 # cluster at school cut-off
)

etable(iv_fit, se = "cluster")

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness check 1: quadratic polynomial & half bandwidth
# -------------------------------------------------
rd_rb <- rdrobust(
  y = dat$test_score_post,
  x = dat$margin_c,
  fuzzy = dat$z_offer,
  p = 2,
  h = bw / 2
)

summary(rd_rb)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness check 2: placebo test on pre-treatment score
# -------------------------------------------------
rd_placebo <- rdrobust(
  y = dat$test_score_pre,   # last-year test (should not jump)
  x = dat$margin_c,
  fuzzy = dat$z_offer,
  p = 1,
  h = bw
)

summary(rd_placebo)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------
Theory/prior empirical evidence (peer quality, resource differences, student–school match) suggest a positive effect. I expect:

• Short-run test scores: +0.07 to +0.12 SD for marginal admittees.  
• Medium-run GPA: +0.05 GPA points.  
• High-school graduation: +2–4 pp.  

Effects may be larger for low-income or historically underserved groups due to bigger differences between preferred and fallback schools.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (FRD)
-------------------------------------------------
C1 (No manipulation of running variable): 1  
C2 (Balance/continuity of covariates): 1  
C3 (Correct bandwidth & polynomial choice): 0.8 (choice is data-driven but model dependence still exists)  
C4 (Exclusion restriction – no other discontinuities): 0.8  
C5 (Sufficient first stage – sizable discontinuity in Pr(treat)): 1  

Total ≈ 4.6 / 5 ➔ high internal validity, subject to standard RD caveats.

-------------------------------------------------
This plan leverages the institutional lottery cut-offs to produce credible causal estimates of how attending a more-preferred school affects subsequent academic performance and attainment.
